title: The Relation of Vernier Acuity to Variations in Intensity and Wavelength

payload.title: The Relation of Vernier Acuity to Variations in Intensity and Wavelength
payload.abstract: Clinical relevance: Vernier acuity (VA) is a common clinical metric used to evaluate cortical visual processing and macular health that is relatively independent of typical optical limitations (such as blurring). Background: Past studies have shown that vernier thresholds do not tend to vary according to blur, intensity and spectral content. This last variable, however, is the most inconsistent and has never been measured using relatively narrowband wavelengths. Methods: This study measured vernier thresholds (VT) as a function of wavelength (n = 15) and intensity (n = 5) in healthy young adults (mean age = 24.8 ± 2.3 years) with normal (or near-normal), corrected vision. VTs were tested using backlit apertures. Narrowband stimuli (420–660 nm) and broadband intensities were produced by a 1000 W Xenon arc lamp with interference filters. VTs, defined as the minimum detectable misalignments between two thin rectangular apertures, were recorded using a digital micrometer. Results: VTs did not vary significantly with wavelength (F (6,84) = 1.56, p = 0.17). Similarly, VTs did not vary significantly with the different broadband intensities (F (5,20) = 1.30, p =0.31). Conclusions: The stability of vernier acuity across these conditions indicates that hyperacuity performance is largely invariant to spectral composition and relatively stable across the limited photopic-to-mesopic intensity range that we tested. These findings are consistent with models proposing that vernier acuity depends primarily on post-receptoral neural mechanisms rather than optical or wavelength-dependent retinal factors.

title: Audit-First Recombination for Test-Time LLM Optimization Under Deterministic Verifiers.

payload.title: Audit-First Recombination for Test-Time LLM Optimization Under Deterministic Verifiers.
payload.abstract: Deterministic verifiers make test-time optimization of large language model (LLM) outputs practical, but modern search pipelines still waste budget on candidates that are structurally ineligible for semantic evaluation. Ineligibility includes parse failures, schema violations, and dependency breaks. These dead-on-arrival candidates consume the same scarce backend capacity as informative trials, reduce throughput under rate limits, and make cross-candidate reuse brittle under strict verifiers. We introduce audit-first recombination, a primitive for verifier-backed generation whose central operation is a deterministic compatibility decision for cross-candidate edits before verifier execution. We represent each candidate as an interface-typed reasoning DAG. We emit an untrusted per-edit certificate. We require every nontrivial edit to pass a deterministic structural gate before any verifier execution. The gate checks acyclicity. It checks namespace closure. It checks schema and terminal validity. It checks interface compatibility. The gate certifies structural eligibility only. Correctness remains entirely defined by the external verifier. We instantiate the primitive in Genetic Inference Search (GIS) with certificate-gated recombination (SemanticGraft). We add a stricter deterministic precondition layer (Cert++). Under strictly matched per-instance token budgets that charge all LLM calls, GIS+Cert++ improves accuracy by 4.2-10.3 points over strong same-budget baselines. It reduces wasted verifier executions. On SWE-bench Verified ($n{=}300$), it increases resolved by 7.6 points relative to Agentless. It uses 38% fewer test runs. Targeted audits show that adding Cert++ preconditions consistently reduces runnable-but-mismatched edits without changing the verifier, and that interface extraction degrades gracefully when symbol metadata is sparse. Finally, we report per-edit diagnostics (CertPass, GVR, CUR, PatchSz). They make reuse auditable and falsifiable in deployment.

title: Deep Learning Analysis of Dual-Modality US Videos for the Characterization of Superficial Lymphadenopathy.

payload.title: Deep Learning Analysis of Dual-Modality US Videos for the Characterization of Superficial Lymphadenopathy.
payload.abstract: Purpose To develop and validate a deep learning (DL) model based on dual-modality US videos to differentiate benign from malignant superficial lymphadenopathy (LA) and stratify malignant subtypes. Materials and Methods This multicenter study included patients with pathologically confirmed LA from five centers (June 2019-December 2025). The Dual-Modality US Video Lymphadenopathy Diagnostic Network (DMUVL-DiagNet) integrated B-mode and color Doppler flow imaging videos with basic clinical information. A retrospective video dataset ( n  = 1616) was used for training and internal testing, while external testing used a prospective dual-modality US video set ( n  = 454) and a static US image set ( n  = 1956). Model performance was compared against clinical baseline and US-based DL models and an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted reader study was conducted. Areas under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUCs) were calculated to evaluate diagnostic performance. The study was prospectively registered at the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2400090592). Results Overall, 4026 patients (median age, 52.6 [IQR 41-62] years; 2175 males) were included. DMUVL-DiagNet consistently outperformed clinical and US-based models across all test sets, achieving AUCs of 0.91-0.95 for benign versus malignant classification and 0.87-0.91 for lymphoma versus metastasis classification. The model showed good generalizability (subgroup AUCs, 0.85-0.93) and surpassed the average performance of all radiologist experience groups in both tasks. Additionally, DMUVL-DiagNet assistance improved junior radiologist AUCs from 0.72 to 0.88 and from 0.58 to 0.77 for the two tasks, respectively (all  P  < .001). Conclusion DMUVL-DiagNet enabled accurate characterization of superficial LA and improved junior radiologist diagnostic performance. © The Authors 2026. title: Checklist for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging (CLAIM): Explanation, Elaboration, and Examples.

payload.title: Checklist for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging (CLAIM): Explanation, Elaboration, and Examples.
payload.abstract: The Checklist for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging (CLAIM) provides a structured framework for transparent and reproducible reporting of AI studies in medical imaging. Since its introduction in 2020, CLAIM has been widely adopted by researchers, reviewers, and journal editors, but variability in its interpretation has limited consistent application. In 2024, the CLAIM Steering Committee published an updated checklist developed through a structured Delphi consensus process involving 72 experts across imaging-related medical specialties, AI science, journal editing, and biostatistics. This article provides a detailed explanation and elaboration of each of the 44 items in the CLAIM 2024 Update, clarifying the intent, common misinterpretations, and appropriate implementation of each item. Illustrative examples from the published literature demonstrating adherence to each item are provided in an accompanying Supplement and through a user-friendly online tool at https://rsna.github.io/claim/. The scope of this work spans the full AI study lifecycle covered by CLAIM, from study design and data sourcing to model development, evaluation, and reporting of results. This resource is intended to support authors, reviewers, and editors in the accurate and consistent application of CLAIM, thereby improving the quality, transparency, and reproducibility of AI research in medical imaging.

title: Evaluating the impact of social determinants of health on model performance and fairness in artificial intelligence for glaucoma progression prediction.

payload.title: Evaluating the impact of social determinants of health on model performance and fairness in artificial intelligence for glaucoma progression prediction.
payload.abstract: To evaluate the impact of incorporating community-level social determinants of health (SDoH) on the performance and algorithmic fairness of artificial intelligence (AI) models trained to predict glaucoma progression to surgery. This multicenter study included 63 268 glaucoma patients across 12 centers. Using electronic health records and community-level SDoH features (Distressed Communities Index [DCI] and rural-urban commuting area [RUCA] codes), we developed XGBoost models to predict progression to incisional glaucoma surgery. We compared SDoH-unaware and SDoH-aware models across an internal test set and 3 diverse external test sets, evaluating area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) (performance) and generalized equalized odds (GEO) (fairness). Including SDoH features resulted in negligible changes in predictive performance across the internal and all external test sets. However, the SDoH-aware model improved algorithmic fairness (achieving lower GEO scores) in the internal set (0.098 vs 0.216) and a mixed-population external site (0.172 vs 0.378). Conversely, inclusion of SDoH marginally improved at a highly urbanized, low-DCI external site (0.491 vs 0.504) and failed to improve at a rural, high-DCI external site (0.241 vs 0.228). Incorporating SDoH features can improve algorithmic fairness regarding socioeconomic disparities without sacrificing predictive accuracy; however, these benefits do not universally transfer to external sites with demographically dissimilar cohorts. Incorporating community-level SDoH features into glaucoma prediction models improved algorithmic fairness with respect to socioeconomic disparities, without significantly altering predictive accuracy. However, fairness benefits did not universally generalize to demographically dissimilar external cohorts. AI models require rigorous external validation across diverse populations to ensure equity prior to clinical implementation.

title: MADE: leveraging informative missingness and temporal evaluation for electronic health record-based deterioration prediction in general wards.

payload.title: MADE: leveraging informative missingness and temporal evaluation for electronic health record-based deterioration prediction in general wards.
payload.abstract: Electronic health record (EHR) time series are irregularly sampled and frequently incomplete, with missingness potentially carrying clinically informative signals. We developed Masked-Attention-based timestamp-wise Data Embedding (MADE), a missingness-aware model for continuous prediction of deterioration in general wards, and evaluated it across heterogeneous hospitals. Observed variables were tokenized into feature-specific embeddings and processed by a masked-attention Transformer, followed by bi-LSTM temporal aggregation for risk prediction. MADE was evaluated for major adverse event (MAE) and sepsis in 1 internal (SVH) and 2 external cohorts (AMC, HUMC) against conventional and deep learning baselines. Ablation studies compared no imputation with last observation carried forward (LOCF) and multiple imputations by chained equations (MICE). Discriminative performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and precision-recall curve (AUPRC). Clinical utility and reliability were assessed using decision curve analysis, Brier score, and expected calibration error (ECE). MADE achieved strong discrimination for MAE (AUROC 0.966/0.902/0.825 for SVH/AMC/HUMC) and sepsis (AUROC 0.934/0.874/0.776). The no-imputation configuration generally outperformed LOCF and MICE, particularly for MAE and for sepsis AUPRC, supporting preservation of informative missingness. Decision curves showed favorable net benefit for MAE and competitive benefit for sepsis. Calibration indicated modest underestimation at higher risks, suggesting site-specific recalibration. MADE mitigates limitations of fixed grid and imputation-dependent EHR modeling by jointly leveraging observed values and missingness patterns under heterogeneous sampling. MADE supports scalable observation-aligned risk monitoring, particularly for MAE, while sepsis prediction may require site-specific recalibration or feature-set adaptation under cross-institution domain shifts.

title: Assessing and improving data quality in health registries: a systematic review of dimensions, frameworks, and artificial intelligence-enabled approaches.

payload.title: Assessing and improving data quality in health registries: a systematic review of dimensions, frameworks, and artificial intelligence-enabled approaches.
payload.abstract: To systematically synthesize how data quality (DQ) in disease and health outcomes registries has been conceptualized, assessed, and improved, emphasizing artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning methods within registry-based DQ workflows. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a comprehensive search was conducted across PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar, and Google through October 26, 2025. Eligible studies evaluated DQ dimensions, frameworks, methods, tools, or algorithms in structured health registries using conventional or AI-based approaches. Methodological quality was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Findings were synthesized using qualitative thematic analysis. A total of 119 studies were included. Completeness (111 studies, 93.3%) and accuracy (93 studies, 78.2%) were the most frequently assessed DQ dimensions, whereas representativeness and coverage were less frequently evaluated. Conventional rule-based, statistical, and audit approaches remained dominant. Artificial intelligence/machine learning methods were applied selectively for anomaly detection, missing-data tasks, record linkage, and automated data extraction. However, implementation remained constrained by heterogeneous data structures, limited interoperability, and insufficient reference standards. Reported limitations most commonly involved methodological and analytical constraints, incomplete data capture, and restricted source verification. Frameworks were predominantly assessment-oriented, with limited integration of lifecycle-based quality management strategies. Despite increasing interest in AI-enabled DQ improvement, registry quality management remains retrospective, fragmented, and insufficiently integrated with lifecycle-oriented infrastructures. Advancing registry DQ requires a transition from retrospective validation toward proactive, lifecycle-integrated, and AI-enabled quality ecosystems. Registry-specific frameworks, interoperable infrastructures, and benchmarking strategies are essential to support scalable and trustworthy registry data systems. CRD420251176960 (https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251176960).

title: Evaluation of an automated workflow for TSN-based bounded-latency communication in ISO IEEE 11073 SDC-based medical networks.

payload.title: Evaluation of an automated workflow for TSN-based bounded-latency communication in ISO IEEE 11073 SDC-based medical networks.
payload.abstract: Interoperable, vendor-independent communication between medical devices in operating rooms has been enabled by the ISO IEEE 11073 Service-oriented Device Connectivity (SDC) standard since 2019. However, mechanisms for predictable and deterministic transmission behavior have not yet been standardized. One approach to enable bounded-latency communication is the use of Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN), an extension of standard Ethernet that enables time-synchronized and controlled data transmission to achieve reliable and time-deterministic data delivery. We implemented and evaluated the integration of TSN into SDC-based medical networks to provide bounded-latency communication through time-division mechanisms. An automated process was developed to extract transmission requirements from SDC devices and generate TSN configuration files for network deployment. The evaluation was conducted in a prototype SDC network under realistic traffic conditions. Furthermore, an SDC library designed with the aim of enabling faster data transmission via QUIC was used in the evaluation. Automated TSN configuration is technically feasible and can improve bounded-latency communication in busy networks. With appropriately dimensioned schedules, the maximum SDC latency remains within the same range under high background traffic as under unloaded conditions. However, improperly dimensioned transmission windows can cause instability, connection loss and latency peaks of up to four times the planned transmission time. SDC with TSN offers a promising approach for achieving bounded-latency communication in interoperable medical networks. Further optimization is required to eliminate latency peaks and meet the timing requirements of safety-critical medical applications.

title: Fundamental kinematic indicators predict surgical expertise and clinical outcomes in robot-assisted surgery.

payload.title: Fundamental kinematic indicators predict surgical expertise and clinical outcomes in robot-assisted surgery.
payload.abstract: The global proliferation of robotic surgical platforms necessitates a framework for objective skill assessment using fundamental kinematic features that are theoretically extractable from any robotic system with 3D position tracking. Here, we demonstrated that fundamental three-dimensional movement patterns alone can accurately distinguish surgical expertise and show associations with clinical outcomes. A Random Forest classifier discriminated expertise with high case-wise accuracy (area under the curve 0.892 ± 0.075), and feature-importance analysis identified left-hand peak density as the principal discriminator. A small set of these fundamental indicators generalized to unseen surgeons in leave-one-surgeon-out validation, localizing the expertise-associated signal to a few interpretable kinematic measures. Kinematic patterns were correlated with clinical outcomes, and exploratory analysis revealed associations between movement features and blood loss. Individual learning curve analysis revealed heterogeneous adaptation patterns among experts transitioning to the new platform and identified distinct phenotypes with implications for personalized training. These findings show that fundamental kinematic analysis using only three-dimensional positional data can provide interpretable indicators of surgical performance that may extend across robotic systems providing coordinate data.

title: RACR-MIL: Rank-aware contextual reasoning for weakly supervised grading of squamous cell carcinoma using whole slide images.

payload.title: RACR-MIL: Rank-aware contextual reasoning for weakly supervised grading of squamous cell carcinoma using whole slide images.
payload.abstract: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is one of the most common cancer subtype, with an increasing incidence and a significant impact on cancer-related mortality. SCC grading using whole slide images is inherently challenging due to the lack of a standardized grading protocol and substantial tissue heterogeneity. We propose RACR-MIL, a weakly-supervised SCC grading approach that achieves robust generalization across multiple anatomies (skin, head & neck, lung). RACR-MIL is an attention-based multiple-instance learning framework that introduces two key innovations for learning grade-specific contextual representations: (1) a hybrid WSI graph that captures both local tissue context and non-local phenotypic dependencies between tumor regions, and (2) rank-ordering constraints on the attention mechanism that encourage consistent prioritization of higher-grade tumor regions and improves region-level grade confidence, aligning with pathologists' diagnostic process. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple SCC datasets, achieving 3%-9% improvements over existing methods and up to 10% improvement in tumor localization. In a pilot study, pathologists reported that RACR-MIL improved grading efficiency in 60% of cases, underscoring its potential as a clinically viable cancer diagnosis and grading assistant.

title: From Laboratory to Real World: A New Benchmark Towards Privacy-Preserved Visible-Infrared Person Re-Identification

payload.title: From Laboratory to Real World: A New Benchmark Towards Privacy-Preserved Visible-Infrared Person Re-Identification
payload.abstract: Aiming to match pedestrian images captured under varying lighting conditions, visible-infrared person re-identification (VI-ReID) has drawn intensive research attention and achieved promising results. However, in real-world surveillance contexts, data is distributed across multiple devices/entities, raising privacy and ownership concerns that make existing centralized training impractical for VI-ReID. To tackle these challenges, we propose L2RW, a benchmark that brings VI-ReID closer to real-world applications. The rationale of L2RW is that integrating decentralized training into VI-ReID can address privacy concerns in scenarios with limited data-sharing regulation. Specifically, we design protocols and corresponding algorithms for different privacy sensitivity levels. In our new benchmark, we ensure the model training is done in the conditions that: 1) data from each camera remains completely isolated, or 2) different data entities (e.g., data controllers of a certain region) can selectively share the data. In this way, we simulate scenarios with strict privacy constraints which is closer to real-world conditions. Intensive experiments with various server-side federated algorithms are conducted, showing the feasibility of decentralized VI-ReID training. Notably, when evaluated in unseen domains (i.e., new data entities), our L2RW, trained with isolated data (privacy-preserved), achieves performance comparable to SOTAs trained with shared data (privacy-unrestricted). We hope this work offers a novel research entry for deploying VI-ReID that fits real-world scenarios and can benefit the community.

title: Operationalizing the EU AI Act in a comprehensive cancer center through an institutional governance framework.

payload.title: Operationalizing the EU AI Act in a comprehensive cancer center through an institutional governance framework.
payload.abstract: The EU AI Act subjects high-risk clinical AI systems to deployer obligations whose institutional operationalization remains undefined. Drawing on experience at a French comprehensive cancer center, we present a governance framework combining three novel components: a dual-axis model for institutional risk stratification, a five-category AI-related adverse event taxonomy inspired by pharmacovigilance, and structured proficiency testing against simulated AI errors. Successful AI integration depends on institutional readiness, not algorithmic performance.

title: Influence of physician and consumer demographics on AI-use penalties in primary care: a vignette-based study.

payload.title: Influence of physician and consumer demographics on AI-use penalties in primary care: a vignette-based study.
payload.abstract: We investigated how the "AI-use penalty"- physicians disclosing AI use being perceived more negatively-is affected by physician and consumer demographics in primary care settings. Participants (N = 1030) assessed fictitious family doctor advertisements varying in AI-use and demographics. Physicians stating that they use (vs. never use) AI were rated as less warm and competent, with reduced appointment willingness. Effects were stronger among younger participants but largely independent of physician demographics.

title: Association of virtual nursing implementation with documentation completeness and interruptions in emergency departments.

payload.title: Association of virtual nursing implementation with documentation completeness and interruptions in emergency departments.
payload.abstract: Virtual nursing (VN) is an increasingly popular nursing care model being implemented nationally to help alleviate nursing burden and shortages which are particularly prevalent in emergency care. This study aimed to evaluate the impact on documentation-related and workflow outcomes among adult patients admitted through the emergency department (ED) who received either a traditional in-person admission assessment or a VN admission assessment. Outcomes included admission assessment duration, documentation completeness, and number of interruptions. This study was a non-randomized retrospective cohort study of adult patients over the age of 18 seen in the ED of 2 Southeastern hospitals and subsequently admitted for inpatient care. Retrospective data were extracted from the EHR and included patients seen in the ED and subsequently admitted from August 2022 through December 2023. Patients who utilized VN for their admission had an overall longer admission assessment duration (on average 3.16 minutes longer). Virtual nursing admission assessments were associated with a statistically significant increase in the number of completed admission assessment tasks and a significant reduction in the number of admission interruptions compared to in-person encounters. Virtual nursing for admission assessments was associated with greater documentation completeness and fewer interruptions, with only a modest increase in assessment duration. These findings highlight the potential of VN to help mitigate the challenges associated with nursing shortages and interruptions in emergency care settings.

title: Association of medical discrimination and hypertension in adults in the All of Us Research Program.

payload.title: Association of medical discrimination and hypertension in adults in the All of Us Research Program.
payload.abstract: To examine the associations of medical discrimination with hypertension (HTN) outcomes. Using cross-sectional data from the All of Us Research Program (2018-2022), we defined elevated blood pressure (BP) as systolic BP ≥130 or diastolic BP ≥ 80 mm Hg. We defined HTN diagnosis as either (1) self-reported HTN or (2) a HTN billing code. Among participants with HTN, we assessed antihypertensive medication use and HTN control. Logistic regression models estimated the associations of medical discrimination (using the Discrimination in Medical Settings Scale) with each BP outcome. The full sample included 29 805 adults, of whom 10 359 adults had elevated BP. Medical discrimination was associated with higher odds of elevated BP (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 1.05, 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.02-1.08) and HTN diagnosis (AOR 1.06, 95% CI, 1.02-1.10). Among participants with HTN, medical discrimination was not associated with treatment or control. Findings suggest that medical discrimination contributes to increased prevalence of elevated BP and HTN diagnosis. Researchers should examine mechanisms linking medical discrimination with HTN.

title: Sustainable artificial intelligence in global health: balancing promise, equity, and environmental realities in low- and middle-income countries.

payload.title: Sustainable artificial intelligence in global health: balancing promise, equity, and environmental realities in low- and middle-income countries.
payload.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in global health informatics is accelerating, yet scaling, sustainability, equity, and environmental challenges limit impact, particularly in Low and Middle Income Countries (LMICs). Drawing on experience from members of the American Medical Informatics Association Global Health Informatics and Climate, Health and Informatics Working Groups, we synthesized implementation, evaluation, sustainability, and governance considerations for AI in resource constrained health systems. We propose a framework integrating four components: Green AI necessity assessments; a One Digital Health systems lens; pragmatic, workflow integrated evaluation; and federated governance supporting locally led stewardship and cross institutional learning. Sustainable AI requires moving beyond short term pilots to address infrastructure, environmental costs, workflow integration, equity, and locally relevant evidence. Funders and implementers should prioritize durable infrastructure, strengthened health information systems, rigorous evidence generation, environmentally responsible deployment, and local stewardship to achieve scalable, equitable, and sustainable AI in global health.

title: Institutional approaches to artificial intelligence policy and guidance in health informatics and information management education: emerging trends and inconsistencies.

payload.title: Institutional approaches to artificial intelligence policy and guidance in health informatics and information management education: emerging trends and inconsistencies.
payload.abstract: To examine the characteristics, scope, and thematic content of institutional and program-level academic artificial intelligence (AI) policies and guidance documents used by CAHIIM-accredited Health Informatics (HI) and Health Information Management (HIM) master's programs in the United States. This convergent mixed‑methods study examined publicly available AI‑related documents (eg, student handbooks, integrity policies, program manuals) from all 48 CAHIIM‑accredited HI and HIM master's programs listed in November 2025. Forty programs (83%) had at least 1 qualifying document, 8 programs had no qualifying documents. Quantitative analyses summarized policy characteristics and examined associations with delivery modality using Fisher's exact tests. Qualitative analysis applied Latent Dirichlet Allocation topic modeling to identify recurring semantic themes across policy texts. Most documents provided guidance rather than formal policies; neither policy type nor audience differed by delivery mode. Content emphasized academic integrity, responsible AI use, and expectations for student conduct. References to privacy, intellectual property, and regulatory concepts were present but less common than academic integrity-related themes. Topic modeling identified 4 dominant themes: academic integrity and appropriate AI use; generative AI in teaching; AI and data‑tool use in research; and student engagement with conversational AI systems. AI guidance and policy are available across most accredited HI and HIM master's programs; however, they vary in structure and scope. The majority of documents emphasize academic integrity and responsible AI use. Future research could examine how academic program AI policies relate to distinct but related domains such as curriculum development and organizational AI governance.

title: Validating DigiHEALTHQUAL for measuring digital health effects on service quality in outpatient care in Germany.

payload.title: Validating DigiHEALTHQUAL for measuring digital health effects on service quality in outpatient care in Germany.
payload.abstract: The adoption of digital health solutions (DHS) in outpatient care is hindered by uncertainty regarding their non-clinical effects and a lack of validated instruments for standardized evaluation. Health care service quality (HCSQ) provides a theoretically grounded framework for assessing these effects, but no validated HCSQ-based instrument has been established. This study aimed to quantitatively validate DigiHEALTHQUAL and compare a theory-derived model structure with a data-derived alternative. We conducted a cross-sectional online survey among 1085 adult patients in Germany with experience using one of four DHS: online appointment booking, digital anamnesis, video consultation, or electronic health records. Psychometric validation included internal consistency analyses, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), exploratory factor analysis (EFA), and comparative model evaluation. The refined theory-derived seven-factor model excluding general satisfaction demonstrated good model fit and strong internal consistency, although discriminant validity between dimensions was limited. EFA yielded a more parsimonious four-factor structure with a dominant process-related factor. High inter-factor correlations supported a higher-order HCSQ structure. Overall, DigiHEALTHQUAL showed validity for assessing non-clinical DHS effects on HCSQ in outpatient care in Germany and supports standardized DHS evaluation in research and practice.

title: Beyond the sycophantic vs. cold divide: towards flexible, emotionally intelligent agents to foster healthier human-AI interactions.

payload.title: Beyond the sycophantic vs. cold divide: towards flexible, emotionally intelligent agents to foster healthier human-AI interactions.
payload.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have only recently become ubiquitous, psychological distress following user-LLM interaction has already been documented in both the scientific literature and the popular media. Such distress may be related to the tendency of some LLMs to provide sycophantic responses that uncritically reinforce the views of the user. To support users’ healthy emotional regulation, flexible, emotionally aware AI systems are needed.

title: Gandalf the Red: Adaptive Security for LLMs

payload.title: Gandalf the Red: Adaptive Security for LLMs
payload.abstract: Current evaluations of defenses against prompt attacks in large language model (LLM) applications often overlook two critical factors: the dynamic nature of adversarial behavior and the usability penalties imposed on legitimate users by restrictive defenses. We propose D-SEC (Dynamic Security Utility Threat Model), which explicitly separates attackers from legitimate users, models multi-step interactions, and expresses the security-utility in an optimizable form. We further address the shortcomings in existing evaluations by introducing Gandalf, a crowd-sourced, gamified red-teaming platform designed to generate realistic, adaptive attack. Using Gandalf, we collect and release a dataset of 279k prompt attacks. Complemented by benign user data, our analysis reveals the interplay between security and utility, showing that defenses integrated in the LLM (e.g., system prompts) can degrade usability even without blocking requests. We demonstrate that restricted application domains, defense-in-depth, and adaptive defenses are effective strategies for building secure and useful LLM applications.

title: MORIC: CSI Delay-Doppler Decomposition for Robust Wi-Fi-based Human Activity Recognition.

payload.title: MORIC: CSI Delay-Doppler Decomposition for Robust Wi-Fi-based Human Activity Recognition.
payload.abstract: The newly established IEEE 802.11bf Task Group aims to amend the WLAN standard to support advanced sensing applications such as human activity recognition (HAR). Although studies have demonstrated the potential of sub-7 GHz Wi-Fi Channel State Information (CSI) for HAR, existing methods often degrade substantially under realistic variations across users, environments, and sensing configurations. This work addresses the poor generalization of Wi-Fi-based HAR by extracting motion-centered representations that reduce dependence on static, environment-specific, and non-activity-related CSI magnitude and phase patterns. CSI signals are transformed into the delay-profile space and decomposed into multiple Doppler velocity projections, which are modeled as observations of a moving point's velocity from different unknown directions, analogous to virtual cameras observing the same motion with varying degrees of clarity. This yields a richer activity representation than either a single aggregated Doppler estimate or the spurious, environment-dependent CSI patterns used in prior works. Since these projections are unordered and may recur due to random multipath propagation, we introduce MORIC, a novel order- and repetition-invariant time-series classification model for robust Wi-Fi-based HAR. Experimental results on the collected dataset show that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in cross-user hand motion recognition, especially for challenging gestures. Incorporating only a few calibration samples further improves accuracy, demonstrating MORIC's adaptability and highlighting the potential of the proposed methodology for practical Wi-Fi sensing in real-world scenarios.

title: Development of a support system for total hip arthroplasty: evaluation of lower limb loads using virtual and dummy human body models.

payload.title: Development of a support system for total hip arthroplasty: evaluation of lower limb loads using virtual and dummy human body models.
payload.abstract: The direct anterior approach (DAA) is one of the procedures used for total hip arthroplasty (THA) and offers advantages such as faster postoperative recovery. A lower limb traction operating table has been developed to assist in intraoperative movement and retention of the lower limb. However, these movements depend on the experience of individual surgeons, and no quantitative safety index is currently available. The authors are developing a surgical support system for THA that evaluates lower limb loads to achieve safe and reliable surgery. This study aimed to establish a system using dummy and virtual human body models that can quantitatively evaluate lower limb loads during procedures. The dummy human body model consisted of a skeletal specimen with six silicone tubes mimicking four types of muscles. Tension sensors were installed to measure tension forces. A virtual human body model with 40 muscles, along with the operating table model, was constructed using the musculoskeletal simulation software OpenSim. The movements of the operating table and the dummy human body model were measured using a 3D motion analysis system, and identical movements were applied for simulation. Traction and extension movements showed that the trend of reaction forces in the traction direction and the relative magnitudes of muscle tension forces in the dummy model were consistent with the simulation results. In addition, the simulation enabled evaluation of muscle forces not physically represented in the dummy model. The validity of the simulation was verified by comparing measured and simulated forces applied to both the virtual and dummy human body models. The combined use of these models enabled evaluation of loads on the sole and muscles surrounding the hip joint. This approach enables quantitative and comprehensive biomechanical evaluation of intraoperative procedures and contributes to the development of a safe surgical support system.

title: Honeycomb-Surfels: Compact Hexagonal Primitives for Efficient Scene Rendering and Reconstruction

payload.title: Honeycomb-Surfels: Compact Hexagonal Primitives for Efficient Scene Rendering and Reconstruction
payload.abstract: Novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction have advanced rapidly with radiance fields and splatting, yet their memory and computational demands limit their use in resource-constrained settings. We introduce Hexels: novel planar hexagonal surface elements with a first-order spatial color field for efficient 3D scene and 2D image representation. Hexels exploit locally planar regions with smoothly varying appearance using fewer, larger primitives. Their hexagonal support provides an area- and boundary-efficient domain, while the local color field captures appearance variation within each primitive. Across 34 scenes, Hexels improve PSNR over memory-matched 2DGS by 4.53-7.38 dB across datasets while requiring lower training VRAM. We further ablate Hexels by showing that per primitive, Hexels outperform 2DGS by upto 4.74 dB while using lower training VRAM and having 2.31 times faster FPS. Even in unconstrained settings, Hexels offers complementary quality-memory trade-offs. For efficient 3D surface reconstruction, Hexels reduce error by 28.9% compared with memory-matched 2DGS across 15 DTU scans. On 6 Tanks and Temples surface scenes, Hexels achieves the highest mean F1 among compared methods (34.38%, versus 31.72% for 2DGS). We further also show that Hexels, as a general primitive, improves 2D image representation over Image-GS. Hexels push the Pareto frontier on the quality-efficiency trade-off of surface-aligned primitives.

title: ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning

payload.title: ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning
payload.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made substantial progress in robotic manipulation, but their generalization remains constrained by the diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Human videos provide much broader behavioral and environmental experience, while learning from them faces a fundamental trade-off between scalable data and explicit action grounding. We introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and strengthens it through reinforcement learning with world imagination. ThinkWorld represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures the intermediate dynamics connecting the current world to a future state and serves as a common action representation across embodiments. We first initialize CoD with action-labeled demonstrations, then predict the future induced by each CoD and reinforce those whose predictions better match the observed outcome. This enables videos without action annotations to provide direct supervision from observed state transitions, allowing human and robot experience to refine the same reasoning space. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate effective human-to-robot transfer and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments.

title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness

payload.title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness
payload.abstract: We introduce Heads of Security (HoS), a prompt injection defense that enforces instruction-data separation via a small set of learned per-head attention gates. HoS learns how each head should redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens, enabling models to reason over untrusted content without following injected instructions. We evaluate HoS on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B. We compare it against SecAlign++, a state-of-the-art finetuning-based defense, and ASIDE, a defense that, like ours, builds instruction-data separation into the model architecture. We show that HoS offers greater robustness to adaptive attacks, better performance on standard utility benchmarks, and matches top performance on standard agentic prompt injection benchmarks. More specifically, the black-box RL-Hammer attack reaches 97% ASR against GPT-OSS-20B and 85% against SecAlign, but only 10% against HoS. Claudini, a state-of-the-art white-box attack, strengthened against HoS through autoresearch, requires 3 times more FLOPs to reach the same ASR on HoS as it does on GPT-OSS-20B or SecAlign. HoS preserves base-model utility across standard multiple-choice benchmarks and prompting setups, whereas SecAlign and ASIDE degrade in few-shot settings. On agentic benchmarks with static attacks, HoS and SecAlign perform similarly and substantially improve the security-utility trade-off over the base model. ASIDE struggles with tool use, achieving only 10% utility. These results show that prompt injection robustness can be achieved and improved through targeted attention interventions.

title: KPPax: preprocess differentiable kinetic ODE for machine learning in atmospheric chemistry

payload.title: KPPax: preprocess differentiable kinetic ODE for machine learning in atmospheric chemistry
payload.abstract: Atmospheric chemical mechanisms are commonly distributed in the language of the Kinetic PreProcessor (KPP), which generates efficient Fortran or C code but does not fit into the differentiable programming frameworks in which machine-learning models are developed. We present KPPax, a kinetic preprocessor that generates differentiable, just-in-time compiled, and vectorisable chemistry code in JAX from mechanisms written in the KPP language. KPPax evaluates the rate law with sparse operations in log space, which keeps it differentiable, and integrates the stiff system with the implicit solvers and the forward- and reverse-mode adjoints of the \texttt{diffrax} library, so that exact sensitivities are obtained without hand-derived adjoint code. We demonstrate two applications with the POLLU benchmark mechanism. In the first, the Fisher information matrix computed from an automatically differentiated Jacobian predicts, before any fit, which of the 25 rate coefficients a flow-tube-like design can identify, and noisy synthetic estimation confirms the predicted uncertainties of the nine identifiable rate coefficients to within about 30\% while revealing clusters of fast reactions of which only ratios are constrained. In the second, a neural-network correction of an emission inventory is trained offline on per-scenario 4D-Var retrievals and then fine-tuned online through the chemical model, which reduces the error of the biogenic correction by a factor of 2.4--5 and recovers information on low-temperature emissions that the individual retrievals lose. KPPax makes KPP mechanisms directly usable for parameter estimation and hybrid physics--machine-learning modelling.

title: Pushing Dexterity and Safety for In-Hand Object Pose Reaching That Works Remarkably Well

payload.title: Pushing Dexterity and Safety for In-Hand Object Pose Reaching That Works Remarkably Well
payload.abstract: Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands is the next frontier of robotics, yet learned hand skills remain limited to simple grasps or basic repeated motions, such as rotating an object. As robots attempt more demanding in-hand maneuvers, safety, such as not dropping the object, becomes critical, yet it is rarely measured. We study in-hand object pose reaching, a task that demands diverse and difficult grasps: moving an object to almost any position and orientation within reach of the fingers, at any wrist orientation, through long sequences of consecutive goals. We present a recipe for training such policies for a LEAP hand in simulation without human data, built on a range of insights, from diverse resets and goals via generated grasp datasets to an adaptive friction curriculum. With careful system identification, the policies transfer zero-shot to the real hand, using either motion capture or a single wrist-mounted depth camera, and prove remarkably capable and robust. On top of the task policy, we add a learned residual safety filter with adjustable conservativeness, letting us tune the balance between performance and safety and greatly reduce object drops. In 13.3 hours of real-robot evaluation over 4,800 unseen goals across 4 objects and diverse wrist orientations, the state-based policy reaches 95.2% of goals within 2 cm and 0.4 rad, and the filter cuts its drops by 75% while still reaching 91.5% of goals. The policies can also spin a lightbulb held in an arbitrary pose, reach out-of-distribution goals, withstand fast arm motion and perturbations, and, needing only a wrist camera, serve as portable skills such as screwing in a lightbulb. We release the full recipe as a platform for studying performance, reliability, and safety in high-dimensional dexterous systems. Videos and more are available at https://ian-chuang.github.io/dexsafe/.

title: Can LLMs Uncover Hidden Physical Laws through Free Exploration?

payload.title: Can LLMs Uncover Hidden Physical Laws through Free Exploration?
payload.abstract: Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation that prompts a new research question. In a world with altered physical laws, can large language models (LLMs) notice unexpected behavior, such as heavier objects falling more slowly, and discover the law through experiments without being told what to investigate? To evaluate this ability, we introduce LongChang, an automated framework that creates simulated worlds with altered physics, where one or more laws differ from ordinary physics. The evaluated LLMs act as explorers, manipulating objects and building tools to investigate their own questions without research tasks or hints about these laws. Separate LLM agents generate and review scenes, review tool designs, and evaluate reports for correctness and experimental support using the altered physical laws and exploration records. These records guide scene evolution for further exploration, allowing the full cycle to run without human intervention. Among 12 LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7%, while the other 11 score 0%. The exploration records reveal uninvestigated anomalies and only partial identification of the altered physical laws.

title: Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions

payload.title: Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions
payload.abstract: When an LLM group's discussion is compressed into a short memory for a final decision maker, what should the memory keep? Two natural heuristics keep the rarest claims or the claims relevant to the decision criteria. On hidden-profile tasks both look attractive, because how widely a fact is held is confounded with whether it helps. We introduce CrossProfile, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 templates with automatically verified answer keys, in which the ownership of supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts is crossed while their text is held fixed (480 tasks). Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and two DeepSeek models, both heuristics fail in predictable places. Selecting by relevance readmits decoys, because decoys are on topic: even a perfect relevance filter loses 23 to 31 points to rarest-first selection in the classic hidden-profile configuration. Rarest-first selection is no better than random selection on average and wins only where the rare facts happen to be the useful ones. In both cases accuracy follows the balance of evidence the memory keeps, not the policy that kept it. The decision model adds a third failure, a form of social proof: it gives extra weight to facts attributed to many agents. Removing the attribution tags, or reassigning them at random with line order fixed, raises accuracy in the classic configuration by 13 to 24 points. In natural discussions the evidence is lost before any memory acts: the complete transcript yields lower accuracy than no notes at all.

title: Perceiving and Predicting Dynamic Sports: Spatiotemporal Intelligence in Vision Models for Egocentric Tennis Video

payload.title: Perceiving and Predicting Dynamic Sports: Spatiotemporal Intelligence in Vision Models for Egocentric Tennis Video
payload.abstract: Agile robots require spatiotemporal intelligence to interpret scenes, reason about interactions, and anticipate future events. Yet it remains unclear how well foundation vision models support these capabilities, particularly from a moving egocentric camera, which is a natural view for robots. To investigate this, we collect an annotated tennis dataset and train a suite of vision models on spatiotemporal tasks. Our dataset contains egocentric video synchronized with five allocentric videos, estimated global positions, labeled contact times, and annotated stroke types. We then evaluate seven prediction tasks from egocentric images: 2D ego player and 3D ball localization, future player and ball trajectories, forehand or backhand stroke anticipation, time to the next ego player ball contact, and 3D ball position at that contact. We compare image encoders, video encoders, and vision-language models with jointly trained prediction heads. The best performing models achieve mean current-frame localization errors of 0.14 m for the ego player and 0.54 m for the ball, future forecasting errors of 0.34 m for the ego player and 0.91 m for the ball over 1.1 s, and a mean contact-time prediction error of 0.14 s. Auxiliary depth information substantially improves 3D ball localization, suggesting that inferring metric depth remains a challenge. Longer image histories do not improve ball forecasting, indicating that representations exploit scene context rather than rely solely on inter-frame motion. Finally, we propose a conditional diffusion model to generate whole-body kinematic tennis motion from vision encoder predictions on egocentric video at real-time rates, adapting movements as predictions are refined. These results move towards a deeper understanding of how foundation vision models can support real-time dynamic robots using egocentric video.

title: EnvSched: Environment-Aware Scheduling for Rollout-Efficient Agent Reinforcement Learning

payload.title: EnvSched: Environment-Aware Scheduling for Rollout-Efficient Agent Reinforcement Learning
payload.abstract: As executable environments for language agents scale, generating and verifying their rollouts becomes increasingly expensive. Under finite rollout budgets, this raises an important question: can data management at the environment level make agentic reinforcement learning (RL) more efficient by organizing, evaluating, and scheduling task instances together with the environments that determine their tools, states, transitions, and verification? To address this question, we introduce EnvSched (Environment-aware Scheduling), an online scheduler that learns from rollout history. EnvSched assigns scheduling value through two complementary modeling choices: exploitation prioritizes tasks likely to provide informative reward differences, while coverage spreads each batch across underobserved environments and interaction patterns. EnvSched organizes environment--task pairs as nodes in a dual-relation graph, with within-environment edges capturing task semantics and shared tool, state, and verifier structure, and cross-environment edges capturing abstract execution and reward topology. By propagating historical rollout statistics along both edge types, it predicts within-task reward variance. These predictions guide a scheduler that allocates each batch to tasks with high predicted reward variance and underobserved environments and tasks. Environment quotas and a similarity penalty further limit concentration and redundancy, yielding informative and diverse batches without additional pilot rollouts. In RL on Qwen3-8B, EnvSched achieves an average score of 48.81 across BFCL-v3, tau-Bench, and ACEBench-Agent after 40 training steps, exceeding the highest score attained by random task selection after 120 steps. It also improves downstream performance across model sizes at the same training budget.

title: Beyond Answer Changes: Matched Same-Class Controls for Local Audio Evidence

payload.title: Beyond Answer Changes: Matched Same-Class Controls for Local Audio Evidence
payload.abstract: For audio-language models, an answer change after a local sound-event edit can reflect a response to the event's class, sensitivity to waveform rewriting, or both. We compare matched same-class and different-class replacements of a queried event. Both use the same interval, level estimate, donor fitting, and crossfade, while the same-class replacement preserves the correct answer. Across 600 synthetic soundscapes and three models from two architecture families, different-class replacements produce 49.7 to 60.9 percentage points more answer changes than same-class replacements. Same-class accuracy remains within 5.2 percentage points of original accuracy. Among trials with correct original and same-class answers, soundscape-weighted selective accuracy for the inserted class is 73.7 to 81.9%, averaging eligible trials within each soundscape and then weighting eligible soundscapes equally. This protocol tests how model answers respond to local changes in event class.

title: MoI-Bench: A Benchmark for Image Generation and Editing on Mobile Devices

payload.title: MoI-Bench: A Benchmark for Image Generation and Editing on Mobile Devices
payload.abstract: Developing on-device image models requires considering practical user needs, task types and device resource constraints. However, existing benchmarks provide limited guidance on identifying capability gaps between on-device models and server-side models. We introduce MoI-Bench, a benchmark grounded in mobile user needs, comprising 64 subtasks and 1150 samples. It defines 16 operations, such as removal and replacement, and eight visual target categories covering content such as portraits and text. These form two orthogonal axes whose applicable combinations define specific tasks, such as removing facial makeup. To better guide model improvement, we further propose MoI-Eval, which introduces task-specific criteria covering instruction following, visual quality and detail preservation. We further construct sample-level evaluation questions and aggregate their scores into overall quality and capability profiles along the operation, target and criteria axes. We evaluate representative on-device and server-side models and measure mobile deployment costs. Results show that this decoupled Operation x Target design provides finer-grained guidance for improving compact models. For example, it highlights the need to prioritize specific capability gaps (e.g., text-replacement) over broad application-level goals (e.g., improving text editing). Unlike conventional benchmarks that rank models using a single score, we introduce a two-dimensional Quality-Deployability capability map to assess models for practical mobile use. The map shows that current on-device models can achieve efficient generation or editing but expanding their task coverage deserves greater attention than further improving deployment efficiency. Further progress requires improving editing quality, particularly identity preservation and text rendering, while broadening task coverage.

title: GAS-PFN: Graph-Aware Spatiotemporal Prior-Data Fitted Networks for Zero-Shot Traffic Forecasting

payload.title: GAS-PFN: Graph-Aware Spatiotemporal Prior-Data Fitted Networks for Zero-Shot Traffic Forecasting
payload.abstract: Traffic forecasting requires modeling complex temporal dynamics and the spatial dependencies imposed by road topology. Supervised graph-based models achieve strong performance, but are often trained for a particular dataset and sensor graph, making deployment to new or evolving networks costly. Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) offer a zero-shot alternative by learning in-context inference from synthetic task priors, which provide an explicit mechanism for encoding domain-specific assumptions. Existing forecasting PFNs, however, do not explicitly represent the graph-structured dependencies governing traffic dynamics. To combine graph-aware traffic modeling with zero-shot adaptation, we introduce the Graph-Aware Spatiotemporal Prior-Data Fitted Network (GAS-PFN). GAS-PFN incorporates sampled road topology into its synthetic task prior through random-walk diffusion, teaching the model to learn graph-coupled dynamics during pretraining. Its co-designed inference architecture uses two mask-conditioned passes through a shared Transformer backbone to separately model sensor-specific temporal dynamics and spatiotemporal interactions among neighboring sensors before integrating their representations for prediction. This design enables GAS-PFN to use target-network structure and context without parameter updates. Across six benchmarks at the 90-minute horizon, GAS-PFN reduces MSE by 34.0% on average relative to TimePFN, its closest PFN-based predecessor. It also reduces MSE by 27.7% on average relative to four recent industry-developed general-purpose zero-shot forecasters. In this comparison, all models receive 90 minutes of contiguous recent history, and any additional context is drawn from each dataset's chronological training split. These results indicate that aligning PFN priors and inference architectures with graph structure improves in-context learning for zero-shot traffic forecasting.

title: Understanding the limits of latent world models

payload.title: Understanding the limits of latent world models
payload.abstract: World models are widely proposed as core components for enabling agents to reason over long temporal and spatial horizons. Yet current evaluations often emphasize task performance while providing limited insight into whether learned world models acquire predictive latent dynamics that reflect the underlying structure of the environment. Here we introduce the concept of faithful latent world models as an equivariance condition between the environment's transition map and the learned latent dynamics. We propose latent rollout consistency (LRC) as a metric to evaluate action-conditioned latent prediction. Strikingly, we find that across the studied state of the art latent world models, none solves the task by actually faithfully modeling the dynamics of the environment.

title: Every route counts, but some count more: a max-plus view of the C. elegans brain

payload.title: Every route counts, but some count more: a max-plus view of the C. elegans brain
payload.abstract: Brains do not simply add up every signal they receive: they select which routes dominate. Yet connectomes are usually analyzed with tools that sum over all paths and place neural states in Euclidean spaces, blurring the feedback circuits that may sustain internal states. Here we treat neural signaling as routing instead of diffusion and describe it with max-plus algebra, in which signals accumulate along a path and the strongest route prevails. We propose a model in which the functional connectome of Caenorhabditis elegans emerges from the time-varying combination of electrical, synaptic, monoaminergic, neuropeptidergic and hormonal layers, and analyze five networks within this framework. Each collapses onto a handful of dominant feedback loops, which recover well-characterized circuits and point to new candidates for experimental study. Unlike linear spectra, these structures keep the biological meaning of the data, and their order-based description suggests that brain states live in lattices rather than Euclidean spaces.

title: REGER: Modeling inter-item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation

payload.title: REGER: Modeling inter-item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
payload.abstract: Personalized recommendation depends on learning semantic and collaborative relations among items from online content and user interactions. Generative recommendation (GR) offers a promising paradigm by autoregressively generating discrete semantic IDs (SIDs) of items. However, randomly initialized SID token embeddings and GR models trained from scratch do not directly inherit the semantic relations inherent in items, while inter-item collaborative relations are learned largely implicitly through token-level attention and next-token supervision. To address this limitation, we propose REGER, a unified framework that explicitly incorporates inter-item relations into semantic pretraining, history encoding, and SID generation. We pretrain the GR model through generative semantic retrieval, enabling it to inherit inter-item semantic similarity by learning to generate semantic neighbors' SIDs. We combine global attention with local attention aligned with SID boundaries to capture historical context and directed transitions between adjacent items. We further develop a theoretical framework for hierarchical preference decomposition over the SID prefix tree, proving an exact factorization of collaborative preference distributions and a weighted decomposition of item-level KL divergence into prefix-conditional KL divergences. Building on this analysis, we distill a discriminative teacher's full conditional distributions over all legal next tokens at ground-truth prefixes along the target SID path, jointly optimizing this objective with cross-entropy. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over existing GR baselines and support the effectiveness of the proposed preference distillation.

title: Zero-Shot Multimodal Event Spotting in Soccer Broadcasts

payload.title: Zero-Shot Multimodal Event Spotting in Soccer Broadcasts
payload.abstract: Automatic soccer event spotting supports highlight generation, video indexing, and sports analytics, but existing methods depend on large annotated datasets and soccer-specific training. We present a zero-shot framework that detects, classifies, and temporally localizes events in full-length soccer broadcasts without task-specific parameter training. Each match is segmented into overlapping clips represented by a compact visual storyboard and the aligned commentary transcript, which a general-purpose multimodal model processes jointly. On three manually annotated matches containing 130 events, the best configuration achieves 72.0% F1@5s and outperforms SoccerNet-trained CALF and NetVLAD++ in a cross-dataset setting, while the storyboard representation reduces inference cost by 72% compared with individual frames. We further analyze the effects of model family, input representation, and prompt optimization, and introduce an evidence-grounded excitement-scoring stage that ranks detected events with natural-language explanations for highlight selection.

title: Spectral Braids: A Topological Descriptor for Dynamic Directed Networks

payload.title: Spectral Braids: A Topological Descriptor for Dynamic Directed Networks
payload.abstract: Eigenvalues are a workhorse of graph machine learning: spectral clustering, spectral graph neural networks, and graph kernels all summarize a network by the eigenvalues of a matrix. These eigenvalues are almost always treated as a static list of numbers. When a graph changes, however, its eigenvalues move, and when the matrix is not symmetric, they move in the complex plane, where they can wind around each other. The pattern of this winding is a braid, a classical object from topology. We propose spectral braids, a methodology for dynamic directed networks: each snapshot is aggregated into a community-level transition matrix, its complex eigenvalues are tracked over time, and the braid they trace is read off as a word. The word is then mapped to a matrix by the Burau representation, which gives a fixed-size feature vector for any classifier. The braid has a concrete meaning: each eigenvalue describes how a group of communities behaves, and each crossing records one group overtaking another. We evaluate the method on dynamic network classification, using synthetic networks of online communities whose labels describe how the network evolved between the same starting and ending states. Our experimental results show that the proposed features reach 97.1% accuracy on four classes, against 44.5% for the best feature set that does not track eigenvalues, and that the Burau features also separate networks containing the same events in a different order, which simple counts of crossings cannot do. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study that defines braids and braid monodromy on graph data and uses them as features for learning on dynamic networks.

title: As the Story Unfolds: Watching a Film and Identifying Characters as a Human Does

payload.title: As the Story Unfolds: Watching a Film and Identifying Characters as a Human Does
payload.abstract: Films introduce characters incrementally as they progress. We study the problem of identifying principal characters and assigning their names directly from the movie itself, without using external cast lists, actor photographs, or pre-built character banks. We introduce the character naming task: given a name mentioned in dialogue and the associated video context, the model must determine which visible character bears that name. This task is challenging because name resolution often depends on cinematic cues such as shot-reverse-shot structure, self-introduction, direct address, third-party reference, gaze, and temporal continuity. We provide a dataset and annotations for evaluating character naming and first character appearances, develop a video-and-dialogue model for the task, and compare it with proprietary multimodal large language models. We further introduce a progressive framework for building a character bank as the film unfolds. Together, these contributions support online, human-like movie understanding in which character identities are inferred from the film itself.

title: TeamGym: A Gym for Team Decision-Making by AI Agents with Distributed Information

payload.title: TeamGym: A Gym for Team Decision-Making by AI Agents with Distributed Information
payload.abstract: Many real-world decisions require teams to integrate information distributed across participants. Yet AI agents are still primarily trained and benchmarked in isolation. We introduce TeamGym, an environment for evaluating and training language model-based agents on team decision-making problems constructed from real-world legal, finance, medical, and software engineering corpora. TeamGym introduces a method to identify a minimal set of facts, each element of which is necessary and all of which are collectively sufficient for a correct final decision, which we call pivotal information. This enables TeamGym to both control the distribution of pivotal information and track how well agents identify and integrate pivotal information when making team decisions. Examining 8 language models on 12 source corpora, we find that current AI agents often fail to effectively share information: Distributing pivotal information across participants lowers success rate by 22.9 percentage points on average relative to giving the same information to a single model (a communication gap). We also document that participants do not effectively retrieve decision-relevant information on their own: A team's success rate is lowered by a further 19.9 points when participants must identify and extract pivotal information from source material rather than receiving it directly (a retrieval gap). To help remedy these deficits, we use TeamGym to train policies through reinforcement learning on team decision loss. Across two policy-training experiments, we find that training improves final-decision quality and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication, even though the reward evaluates only the final decision.

title: LCM-Promo: An LLM-Based Uplift Model for Promotion Allocation

payload.title: LCM-Promo: An LLM-Based Uplift Model for Promotion Allocation
payload.abstract: We present LCM-Promo, an LLM-based uplift model for promotion allocation. LCM-Promo is a task-specific Large Commerce Model (LCM): a finetuned LLM trained on transactional commerce data to predict user intent and promotion response. It learns monotonic promotion-response curves from production logs by interpreting single-token outputs as conversion-threshold probabilities, while conditioning on session context such as day and delivery shift. In a production A/B test on churn reactivation, LCM-Promo increased conversion by 1% and reduced promotion cost by 6% relative to the Segment-EMA production baseline.

title: Pneuma: A Large-Scale Real-World Time Series Benchmark for Commercial Aircraft Predictive Maintenance

payload.title: Pneuma: A Large-Scale Real-World Time Series Benchmark for Commercial Aircraft Predictive Maintenance
payload.abstract: Predictive maintenance is vital for commercial aviation, yet progress remains hindered by the lack of public, large-scale real-world datasets. As a result, most methods are developed and evaluated on proprietary data, limiting reproducibility. We introduce Pneuma, the first publicly available large-scale benchmark for predictive maintenance using onboard time series from in-service commercial aircraft. Built around bleed air systems, Pneuma contains over 920 million multivariate time steps across four aircraft types and 9 verified fault scenarios, directly aligned with real maintenance logs. The dataset exhibits key real-world challenges, including substantial class imbalance, subtle fault evolution patterns, and significant variance across aircraft configurations. We structure the benchmark around three tasks: multivariate forecasting, supervised fault classification, and unsupervised anomaly detection, with labels derived from actual maintenance records. Under unified settings, we evaluate over 25 models from four methodological families on 9 carefully curated subsets. The results reveal that even strong contemporary models struggle with subtle fault signatures. Further analyses show consistent gains from additional in-context examples and multivariate inference, while forecasting quality is strongly associated with anomaly detection performance. Together, these findings provide practical insights into effectively modeling complex real-world aviation time series. We hope Pneuma will serve as a rigorous and reproducible foundation for advancing data-driven predictive maintenance toward real-world deployment in commercial aviation.

title: Kinematic Constraint-Referenced Evaluation for Articulated Object Manipulation

payload.title: Kinematic Constraint-Referenced Evaluation for Articulated Object Manipulation
payload.abstract: Manipulation policies are evaluated predominantly by binary task success, which cannot tell whether the commanded gesture is the one the object's kinematics admit. We introduce Constraint-Referenced Strategy (CRS), which projects the commanded end-effector twist onto the object's joint axis, separating progress along the joint from off-constraint waste. CRS requires a joint model and a joint-following scripted controller derived from it, but no recorded demonstration or learned judge. On 74 simulated articulated objects, success registers three transfer failures as lower rates but attributes none, while the two CRS channels give each a distinct signature. A door-trained behavior-cloning policy opens drawers in 59 of 110 episodes, and in these passes it commands about $40\times$ the off-axis rotation of a drawer-trained policy's passes ($1.27$ vs.\ $0.032$~rad/s). Relative to a scripted controller scored with the same axis, CRS verdicts are unchanged under joint-axis errors up to $30^\circ$; absolute thresholds tolerate about $8^\circ$.

title: When, Where, and What to Correct: Human-Guided Adaptive Residual Correction for Robot Policies

payload.title: When, Where, and What to Correct: Human-Guided Adaptive Residual Correction for Robot Policies
payload.abstract: Imitation policies that reliably execute most of a manipulation trajectory can still fail in localized regions requiring last-mile precision. Updating the full policy or exploring residual actions everywhere treats this local failure as a global learning problem. We introduce Adaptive Residual Correction (ARC), a lightweight post-training module that uses reinforcement learning (RL) to learn a residual correction on top of a frozen policy while using sparse human corrections to structure autonomous exploration. Rather than treating human corrections as imitation targets, ARC uses pre-intervention states to determine 'when' residual control should become active and correction geometry to determine 'where' in residual action space autonomous refinement should explore; task reward determines 'what' residual is ultimately executed. Across three precision-manipulation tasks on a real robot, ARC improves average task success from 33.3% to 75.0%. The human corrections define task-dependent 2-3 dimensional subspaces of the seven-joint residual space that retain 96.0-97.7% of squared correction magnitude. Together, these results show that sparse human corrections can localize and constrain autonomous post-training without requiring the observed correction itself to serve as the final action target.

title: GroundControl: Satellite-Conditioned Multi-View Diffusion for Reconstruction-Free Novel View Synthesis

payload.title: GroundControl: Satellite-Conditioned Multi-View Diffusion for Reconstruction-Free Novel View Synthesis
payload.abstract: Multi-view or video diffusion models have recently emerged as state-of-the-art approaches for novel-view synthesis from sparse image collections. While they can produce high quality images, they tend to hallucinate unrealistic spatial layouts when synthesizing views outside the input views (scene extrapolation). We propose to address this challenge for outdoor scenes by using satellite images as an additional information source to condition the multi-view generative model. We introduce a new satellite-conditioned multi-view diffusion model that combines conditioning from a satellite image and street-level input images when generating novel-views. Our cross-attention based conditioning allows us to retain pretrained multi-view diffusion priors to generate seamless, realistic, novel views from a handful of source views, while also adhering to the scene layout as seen from satellite images. Our model does not use 3D scene reconstruction, and only relies on posed street and satellite views. Our experiments on outdoor datasets show that our model is better than both satellite-conditioned or street-view conditioned baselines on novel-view synthesis, especially on challenging cases where target views have very little overlap with source views. Project page: https://nianticspatial.github.io/groundcontrol

title: GTFormer: A Syntax-Free Graph Network Alternative to Transformers for 8192$\times$ Length Extrapolation in Linear Time

payload.title: GTFormer: A Syntax-Free Graph Network Alternative to Transformers for 8192$\times$ Length Extrapolation in Linear Time
payload.abstract: Self-attention mechanisms have established the Transformer as the dominant backbone across natural language processing, source code intelligence, and automated theorem proving. However, all-to-all pairwise token comparison enforces a quadratic $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ compute and memory barrier alongside severe softmax attention dilution as sequence length $N$ scales beyond the training horizon. Inspired by recent advances in algebraic graph learning (\textbf{WPNet}), this work introduces \textbf{GTFormer}, a syntax-free hierarchical Graph Neural Network (GNN) that replaces flat self-attention for general long-context sequence modeling. GTFormer organizes raw token streams into a bounded-degree hierarchy combining a balanced binary reduction tree ($\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ depth), horizontal boundary-bridging shift edges, random expander shortcuts, multi-channel convex highway gating, and a top-down broadcast pass. Across eight long-context code, log, and multi-hop retrieval benchmarks trained exclusively on sequences of length $N \le 512$, GTFormer extrapolates zero-shot to $N = 4{,}194{,}304$ ($8192\times$) on a single commodity GPU in linear $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, maintaining near-perfect accuracy where standard and RoPE Transformers suffer from out-of-distribution attention collapse and out-of-memory exhaustion.

title: Strategyproof Deep Reinforcement Learning for Online Resource Allocation

payload.title: Strategyproof Deep Reinforcement Learning for Online Resource Allocation
payload.abstract: Online resource allocation faces two coupled challenges: (1) allocating scarce resources efficiently under uncertain future demand, and (2) ensuring that agents report task valuations and requirements truthfully (strategyproofness).
