To rule out correspondences that are cycle-consistent but physically implausible, we introduce a Doppler consistency loss that constrains correspondence-induced motion using radial velocity measured by the RF sensor itself. Ego-motion is then recovered through robust $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ registration that suppresses uncertain correspondences and those arising from independently moving objects. Without pose labels or auxiliary sensors, RFWalk remains competitive with supervised baselines in static scenes and reduces absolute trajectory error by 58% in dynamic scenes with moving pedestrians.

title: AlbumVSR: Identity-Preserving Face Video Super-Resolution from a Personal Photo Album

payload.title: AlbumVSR: Identity-Preserving Face Video Super-Resolution from a Personal Photo Album
payload.abstract: Severe blur, downsampling, noise, and compression can erase the identity cues needed to faithfully restore a person's face. We therefore use photographs of the same person as an external source of identity. AlbumVSR conditions a frozen, one-step streaming diffusion transformer on a personal album. We use four MagFace/CLIP set tokens to encode the album, and 64 texture tokens which come from a fused UV atlas rendered at the current window's estimated face pose. These tokens are appended to the transformer's cached cross-attention context. On an identity-disjoint VoxCeleb2 benchmark with heavy synthetic degradation, AlbumVSR raises ArcFace similarity to the ground truth from 0.586 to 0.670 and face PSNR from 24.98 to 26.71 dB. On the 91 test identities, its mean identity similarity is higher than that of all 14 baselines.

title: Syntactic Segmentation and Collage Generation for Videogame Levels with Perceptual Distance

payload.title: Syntactic Segmentation and Collage Generation for Videogame Levels with Perceptual Distance
payload.abstract: In procedural videogame level design, many existing techniques combine hand-authored level chunks. Some existing analysis techniques also rely on a higher-level graph structure which abstracts the level design. In this paper, we explore techniques for computing both of these things automatically from an existing design. We introduce the concept of perceptual distance, based on analysis techniques from the architecture subfield of Space Syntax. We use this perceptual distance to segment level designs with hierarchical clustering. We compare with past work on StarCraft analysis, show results on rooms from Super Metroid, and also demonstrate a proof-of-concept level generation algorithm based on this segmentation method.

title: Benchmarking Graph Neural Networks for AC Power Flow: The Role of Inductive Biases and Physical Constraints

payload.title: Benchmarking Graph Neural Networks for AC Power Flow: The Role of Inductive Biases and Physical Constraints
payload.abstract: Fast and accurate models for AC power flow (ACPF) are increasingly important as modern electrical grids require more frequent system analyses. Graph neural networks (GNNs) naturally exploit electrical grid topology, yet the effects of architectural design choices on predictive performance remain poorly understood given differences in graph representations and evaluation settings across studies. We present a unified benchmark of representative GNN architectures for ACPF prediction under a common experimental framework. All models use identical preprocessing and training procedures and comparable parameter budgets, isolating the impact of message-passing mechanisms and inductive biases. We also analyze errors by distance from the slack bus and systematically ablate key design components. We evaluate predictive accuracy and physical consistency on the IEEE 14-bus and IEEE 118-bus systems. Results indicate that anisotropic message-passing architectures offer the most favorable trade-off between predictive accuracy and physical consistency under the studied parameter and topology constraints. Explicit edge features encoding line impedances and global context aggregation are particularly important for representing electrical interactions and system-wide dependencies, especially for voltage-angle predictions on the topologically bottlenecked IEEE-118 grid. Under a budget with approximately fixed parameters, two or three message-passing layers generally provide the best balance between depth and representation width, while additional depth offers no consistent improvement. Ablations also show that standard residual and root connections are not necessarily beneficial in shallow models, and that aggregation operators involve trade-offs between statistical accuracy and physical consistency. These results provide practical guidelines for designing graph-based power system models.

title: Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code

payload.title: Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code
payload.abstract: Large language models pass most functional-correctness benchmarks, but passing tests says little about whether their code is readable, efficient or secure. Many techniques claim to improve these qualities, yet their evidence is scattered, usually covers one quality dimension and is rarely compared at an equal compute budget. We contribute a systematic review and a controlled re-evaluation. A systematic literature review of 628 primary studies (July 2021 to October 2026), with disclosed, author-reviewed LLM assistance, organizes the techniques by stage, signal source and quality target. Most studies measure only the dimension they target, gains often come with unchanged or unreported correctness, single automated quality signals are gamed, and compute, variance and contamination are rarely reported. A controlled re-evaluation runs ten techniques on four models at matched budgets on correctness, maintainability, efficiency and security benchmarks, extends it to thirteen current models and repository-level tasks, and compares 66 highlighted techniques head-to-head on Gemma 4 31B. At one call, quality prompting raises analyzer issue counts and leaves complexity and judge scores almost unchanged. At matched budgets, best-of-n sampling with an analyzer-weighted ranker matches or beats prompting, planning, self-refinement, a reviewer agent and retrieval on measures the ranker does not optimize, while an analyzer feedback loop and fine-tuning beat it only on analyzer issue counts. Large correctness losses on HumanEval+, a likely contaminated benchmark near its ceiling, do not appear on contests held after the models' training cutoffs. In the head-to-head, 1 of 66 techniques beats best-of-n on its primary target beyond the 95% interval, a rate consistent with chance. Gains should be reported against a budget-matched sampling baseline and on measures independent of the technique's own signal.

title: The Utility of Physics-Informed Machine Learning in Solar Power Production Forecasting

payload.title: The Utility of Physics-Informed Machine Learning in Solar Power Production Forecasting
payload.abstract: Physics-informed machine learning (PIML) and hybrid modeling have attracted significant attention as approaches for combining physical knowledge with the flexibility of deep learning. In this work, we investigate whether these approaches deliver their commonly claimed benefits for large-scale photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting. We develop two hybrid forecasting architectures that integrate the ADR physical PV efficiency model with the TSMixer neural forecasting architecture through feature augmentation and residual learning. The proposed models are evaluated on a dataset comprising over 3 million samples from 3,713 PV installations across 33 European countries. We assess convergence speed, forecasting accuracy, transferability across geographical regions, and data efficiency. Although the physics-informed models seem to exhibit slightly faster convergence during training, they do not achieve consistent improvements in test-set accuracy, generalization, or performance under limited training data compared to the purely data-driven baseline. These findings suggest that, for modern deep forecasting architectures trained on large datasets, explicitly incorporating the ADR physical model provides limited practical benefit for day-ahead PV forecasting.

title: Dungeons & Dragons Encounter Analysis with Semi-Random Simulation in Foundry VTT

payload.title: Dungeons & Dragons Encounter Analysis with Semi-Random Simulation in Foundry VTT
payload.abstract: Dungeons & Dragons (D&D) is a tabletop roleplaying game (TTRPG) in which a group of players, guided by a Game Master, roleplay a fantasy adventure with simulated combat and improvisational narrative. In D&D, an encounter is a single instance of simulated combat, where the players must use their characters to attempt to defeat a selection of enemy characters that the GM controls. D&D has multiple systems that approximate encounter difficulty by summing individual difficulty values that designers predefine for each enemy. However, since players and enemies can have a wide variety of capabilities, encounter difficulty depends on more than just the estimated difficulty of each monster. For example, these metrics do not account for positioning and dungeon layout, the synergies between monster abilities, and player party composition. We have created a tool, Mage-Hand, that can simulate D&D encounters semi-randomly using Foundry Virtual Tabletop, a virtual tabletop (VTT) system. In this paper, we show that our tool's simulated winrates have a strong correlation with D&D's published difficulty evaluation metrics, while also better aligning with some players' reported experiences.

title: Communication-Efficient Clustered Federated Learning in Non-IID Wireless Networks

payload.title: Communication-Efficient Clustered Federated Learning in Non-IID Wireless Networks
payload.abstract: Current and emerging mobile networks face increasing privacy, scalability, and performance challenges as distributed learning becomes essential for advanced 6G services. These challenges are amplified by the presence of non-IID data, naturally arising in heterogeneous wireless environments, that degrade the performance of standard Federated Learning (FL) approaches. To address non-IID data across clients, we propose a Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) framework that assigns clients to specialized models during training. Data-domain clustering initializes model-based clustering, enabling identification and exploitation of client similarities without sharing raw data while reducing communication cost. Motivated by mmWave beam selection, we evaluate our methods on a wireless simulation dataset (DeepMIMO) and complement it with two non-IID benchmarks (FEMNIST, Rotated CIFAR-10) to isolate different non-IID characteristics. Our best configurations improve accuracy over IFCA by 4.8 pp on DeepMIMO and 10.6 pp on FEMNIST while reducing downlink data volume by 83.1 % on FEMNIST compared to IFCA. We demonstrate that different clustering strategies suit different non-IID characteristics. These results show that our CFL methods enable resource-efficient, and high-performance distributed learning in future 6G networks.

title: TableTune: Measured, Self-Correcting Draft-Length Tables for Dynamic Speculative Decoding

payload.title: TableTune: Measured, Self-Correcting Draft-Length Tables for Dynamic Speculative Decoding
payload.abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model (LLM) serving only while the GPU has spare compute, so the best draft length, the number of tokens a small drafter guesses per step, shrinks as the batch grows. vLLM lets operators set the draft length for each batch size with a hand-written table, but nothing measures or corrects that table. We present TableTune. Its tuner times the decoding step for every batch size and draft length on vLLM's own serving path and computes, in minutes, the table that maximizes throughput. Its controller, a vLLM plugin, tracks how many guesses are accepted in live traffic and rebuilds the table while serving. We measure TableTune only against other ways to speculate. On an H100, the tuned table delivers at least 94% of the throughput of the best fixed draft length at every load in four of five drafter settings (88% in the fifth) without the operator having to know which length that is. Against reimplementations of TurboSpec- and Nightjar-style control on the same engine, its worst-case loss is never higher than theirs, and with the EAGLE-3 drafter it is 3% against 9% and 12%. On a mixture-of-experts model, vLLM's documented table loses up to 18% and the tuned table at most 3%. Starting from mistuned tables, the controller raises throughput by up to 58% (up to 45% on vLLM's default runner), and after a workload switch with the DFlash drafter it recovers 96% of a stale table's loss. In llm-d's optimized-baseline deployment as shipped, two Qwen3-32B replicas on four GPUs, the tuned table is up to 32% faster than a fixed draft length of 3 and up to 25% faster than vLLM's documented table at high load, and the controller raises the documented table's throughput by up to 29%.

title: Planned Restlessness: Delayed Meta Bandits with Budgets

payload.title: Planned Restlessness: Delayed Meta Bandits with Budgets
payload.abstract: We study episodic finite-horizon Bayesian bandits, or meta-bandits, with independent arms. Each episode draws fresh arm qualities from unknown recurring priors. Observations arrive after known delays, and plays obey hard per-episode caps and total budgets. A play earns reward and informs both the current quality and the recurring prior: the learner must explore, use, and generalize. We formulate a common planning optimization over learning trajectories. Its LP relaxation values experiments through current reward, resource consumption and continuation: the value of future decisions from the learning state produced. Dual prices separate the arms into local programs and certify every admissible policy, including hierarchical Thompson sampling. Execution enforces the hard constraints while preserving the promised learning transitions or accounting for their loss. The framework also represents risk-sensitive objectives and prices purchased observations and buyout options. Delayed reports create planned restlessness: an arm's information changes while it is not played, through reports of its own earlier plays arriving on a known calendar. For stationary priors, finite reward alphabets, bounded report lag and nonbinding budgets, posterior sampling over the recurring priors bounds the price of not knowing them by $O(\sqrt{N})$ over $N$ episodes, with other parameters fixed. For one undelayed $T$-step episode with arms capped at $T/X$ plays each, we obtain the LP-relative approximation factor $1+(2πX)^{-1/2}+O(X^{-1})$, improving previous factors, with a matching lower bound for the leading term.

title: GradSplat: Gradients Inside the Forward Pass for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting

payload.title: GradSplat: Gradients Inside the Forward Pass for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
payload.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting predicts a scene from a few images, but our predictor is less accurate than its own Gaussians optimized per scene on those images. This gap lies mostly in the shape of the Gaussians, their scale and rotation, since optimizing the shape alone recovers almost all of it and opacity and color recover less. Gradient steps on the input views correct this shape, and the model holds these views at inference. Log-anisotropy correction changes the axis ratios of each Gaussian in log space at constant volume, and in-forward gradient refinement renders the Gaussians into the input views and applies the gradient of the photometric loss with a learned recurrent update, first to opacity and color and then to the shape. GradSplat is a feed-forward model that refines its own Gaussians by learned gradient steps inside its forward pass, with no target view. On both complete six-view RealEstate10K protocols, it has the best PSNR and SSIM among nine methods and keeps its accuracy from $6$ to $42$ input views. Without fine-tuning, it is the most accurate on DL3DV and has the best PSNR and SSIM on ScanNet++. The code will be released at https://github.com/Jingong-Chen/GradSplat/.

title: MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems

payload.title: MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
payload.abstract: Training-time multi-agent system (MAS) design seeks to learn reusable orchestration policies, yet prevailing approaches remain largely one-shot: an Orchestrator generates a system but only observes and learns from its terminal outcome. This paradigm discards execution trajectories that expose system-level failures and contain fine-grained information beyond the terminal outcome, leaving no direct basis for revising the source MAS, evaluating the updated MAS, or learning from the resulting contrast. To this end, we introduce MAS-Loop, an execution-grounded framework that closes this feedback loop by coupling an Orchestrator with a trajectory-conditioned Refiner. For each task, the Orchestrator constructs and executes a source MAS to obtain an outcome score and an intermediate trajectory. Conditioned on the trajectory, the Refiner localizes an actionable failure, formulates a trajectory-grounded diagnosis, and proposes a bounded patch to the agents, information flow, or execution configuration. The executable updated MAS is re-executed on the same task to measure its realized outcome under stochastic execution. This pair-MAS comparison provides complementary learning signals: the Orchestrator learns to generate strong systems with fewer recoverable failures, whereas the Refiner learns to expose and repair observed weaknesses, thereby driving policy-level co-evolution across training iterations. Experiments show that MAS-Loop achieves the strongest overall performance among the evaluated baselines, with consistent gains from refinement across all evaluated benchmarks. The co-evolution process also yields MAS-JudgeCorpus, a dataset of execution-grounded source-updated pairs with orchestration- and trajectory-level supervision, which can provide the community with support for MAS reward modeling and trajectory-aware investigation.

title: Optimization-based lane-changing trajectory planning in mixed traffic with embedded input convex neural networks

payload.title: Optimization-based lane-changing trajectory planning in mixed traffic with embedded input convex neural networks
payload.abstract: Lane-changing (LC) maneuvers are highly challenging vehicle interactions, with substantial implications for traffic safety and efficiency. Developing effective LC strategies for connected and automated vehicles in mixed traffic is complicated by the uncertainty associated with surrounding-vehicle behavior and the computational burden of embedding realistic prediction models within optimization schemes. To capture these complex interactions while retaining tractability, this study proposes a data-driven optimization framework that embeds neural network (NN) surrogates for safety and lateral comfort within a Bézier-curve-based trajectory planner. Specifically, the safety cost during the LC process is quantified via a surrogate composed of an input convex recurrent neural network (ICRNN) encoding the planned trajectory, a fully input convex neural network (FICNN) embedding the LC duration, and a partially input convex neural network (PICNN) decoder fusing them with historical traffic states; separately, another FICNN surrogate approximates the optimal lateral comfort cost as a function of the LC duration. Both surrogates are embedded via linear programming (LP) formulations, avoiding the binary variables required by conventional mixed-integer programming (MIP) approaches for NN-embedded optimization. We further theoretically establish their exactness at optimality and extend the framework to problems with additional analytical objective terms and multiple surrogates. Experiments on a hybrid dataset combining real-world and simulated trajectories demonstrate that the proposed method achieves surrogate accuracy competitive with unconstrained baselines while substantially improving optimization efficiency over conventional MIPs. Closed-loop simulations further show that the proposed planners markedly reduce the weighted planning cost and consistently outperform baseline methods.

title: TreasuryQA Bench: Can AI Agents Work an Archive of Scanned Financial Records?

payload.title: TreasuryQA Bench: Can AI Agents Work an Archive of Scanned Financial Records?
payload.abstract: Organisations keep decades of financial records as scanned PDFs on shared drives, and AI agents can now reach those drives through Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Existing benchmarks do not mirror this production setting because they simplify the task. In some, the relevant documents are handed to the agent, so it never has to search. In others, the agent searches through documents with pre-extracted text, so it never has to read scanned images. We introduce TreasuryQA Bench, which requires both: 70 questions over 1,435 scanned U.S. Treasury publications, held in Veris's high-fidelity Dropbox twin. In each task the agent searches for the relevant file through Dropbox's MCP server, reads the pages it needs with Reducto's hosted OCR server or its own tools, and replies with one exact figure. A Python grader checks each answer against an accepted range around the correct value. In this paper we present results from ten agents. The best, Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, solves 64.8% of attempts and the worst, GPT-5.6 Terra in Codex, solves 16.7%, so the benchmark is far from saturated. We also test how scan quality affects performance: every agent solves fewer tasks on the blurriest scans. Most failed attempts reply with a wrong number rather than no number, and the most common cause is a digit misread from the scan. Three worked examples are included with their answer keys.

title: TrussTutor-Bench: Benchmarking large language models on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection in statics

payload.title: TrussTutor-Bench: Benchmarking large language models on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection in statics
payload.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly become a default source of help for students in science and engineering courses. In foundational engineering mechanics courses such as statics, students routinely use these tools to check answers, work through partial solutions, and ask for explanations. Effective tutoring in this setting requires more than a correct final answer. A model must also confirm correct work when a student doubts it, and identify errors in flawed work. Existing benchmarks evaluate LLMs primarily on final-answer accuracy, so it is unclear whether models that can solve mechanics problems also have the other technical capabilities that tutoring depends on. Here we introduce TrussTutor-Bench, a benchmark of 200 verified two-dimensional truss problems paired with automatically generated student solutions, and use it to evaluate thirteen LLMs on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection. Baseline accuracy ranged from 64.5% to 97.0%. Every model detected nearly all injected errors in synthetic flawed student work (90.4% to 100%), so error detection did not distinguish models under these clean conditions. Sycophancy did. When a student insisted that correct work was wrong, models rejected correct solutions to problems they had themselves solved in 1.6% to 50.0% of cases. These results show that performance varies widely across models: the leading models solve, check, and defend student work nearly perfectly, while others are far less reliable, particularly when a student doubts correct work. TrussTutor-Bench provides a verified, extensible standard for determining which models are technically reliable enough to put in front of students. Follow-up work must now focus on teaching rather than technical capability, drawing on learning science to determine whether LLM help leads students to understand the material or simply to reach the right answer.

title: Lev-3B: A Data Recipe for Compact Probabilistic Log Decision Models

payload.title: Lev-3B: A Data Recipe for Compact Probabilistic Log Decision Models
payload.abstract: Many log-analysis tasks involve choosing among known options, such as detecting anomalous sessions or identifying attack techniques, and benefit from calibrated probabilities. We present Lev-3B, an open 3B-parameter decision model built on Granite-4.1-3B-Base with a shared pointer readout, and study its training recipe. The recipe has two key parts. First, training follows a curriculum: the model learns bounded natural-language decisions, using no log data, before it sees any logs. Second, the log stage mixes the target tasks with general log data spanning 35 auxiliary tasks unrelated to either evaluation task. We evaluate one shared checkpoint on sources seen in training and on sources excluded from training, calibration and model selection. The two-stage recipe transfers substantially better than training on log data alone. Adding general log data improves performance on excluded sources. At a fraction of their serving cost, Lev-3B outperforms prompted frontier models on anomaly detection, including on an excluded logging system, but trails them on attack-technique classification. Its probabilities are well calibrated on familiar sources, but on the excluded logging system it confidently misses anomalies. We release the checkpoint, recipe, data manifests, and prediction-level artifacts.

title: Geometric Time Score Estimators: Bridging Self-Predictive Representations and Generative Occupancy Models For Reinforcement Learning

payload.title: Geometric Time Score Estimators: Bridging Self-Predictive Representations and Generative Occupancy Models For Reinforcement Learning
payload.abstract: In reinforcement learning (RL), temporal reasoning is essential for estimating the density of future outcomes under a policy's occupancy measure. While self-predictive representations have been a dominant paradigm for occupancy density estimation, we find that they yield surprisingly poor estimates. On the other hand, generative occupancy models can produce remarkably accurate samples from the occupancy measure. Yet, they cannot easily recover occupancy densities, limiting their use for control despite their expressivity. In this paper, we propose Geometric Time Score Estimators (GTSE), a framework that bridges the two paradigms by learning occupancy density estimators along probability paths. We analyze how GTSE implicitly induces better occupancy estimators through improved representation learning and show how to directly extract self-predictive representations from this framework. Through experiments across several locomotion and manipulation tasks, we show that GTSE improves performance over state-of-the-art methods by $2\times$ to $6\times$ in goal-conditioned RL settings, and that the representations learned using our framework transfer effectively to downstream RL tasks. Website: https://aravindvenu7.github.io/website/gtse/

title: Aligning Autoresearch: Co-Improvement between Agents and Humans

payload.title: Aligning Autoresearch: Co-Improvement between Agents and Humans
payload.abstract: Autoresearch agents can now attempt long-horizon AI research end-to-end, i.e., self-improvement. However, best results are still obtained by research agents interacting with human researchers, and improving AI's ability to perform this co-research will only reinforce this effect---a process termed co-improvement (Weston and Foerster, 2025). Further, aligning with human expectations is likely a safer path for research agents, especially given recent agent reward hacking phenomena (OpenAI, 2026b). In this work we address these issues in four ways: (i) we empirically study the role of humans in directing autoresearch agents, focusing on the domain of benchmark creation, and find humans still play a pivotal role particularly in the ideation phase; (ii) we also develop a benchmark, HackBench, that shows current autoresearch agents are not aligned and are unable to achieve hack localization sufficiently; (iii) we present a method to train agents for improved human interaction by using human simulators as a proxy during reinforcement learning (RL); and finally (iv) we develop a method to improve model text generation, and hence agent communication, by RL with rubrics aligned with human experts. Together, our training and evaluation recipes provide a path toward more capable and aligned (co-)research agents.

title: Auditable Belief Updates as a Missing Safety Layer for LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Systems

payload.title: Auditable Belief Updates as a Missing Safety Layer for LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Systems
payload.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as cognitive interfaces that shape how users interpret evidence, communicate, and make decisions. As deployed systems become more multimodal, tool-using, and multi-agent, safety failures no longer arise only from isolated harmful outputs, but also from how agents update, store, and propagate epistemic commitments across retrieval, memory, tools, and peer communication. In this paper, we define belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments that guide downstream action. Building on this view, we propose the Explicit Belief Multi-Agent System (EB-MAS), which externalizes belief states into a structured substrate, uses belief operators to propose candidate updates, and applies a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject updates that are weakly evidenced but strongly driven by vulnerability cues. We also discuss the risk of group belief at the group level, including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation, and outline practical integration challenges around grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse. Therefore, scalable agent safety requires not only better output filtering or stronger base models, but also explicit interfaces for tracing, calibrating, and constraining belief revision at runtime.

title: Where You Inject Matters: The Trust Region Effect in LLM Agents

payload.title: Where You Inject Matters: The Trust Region Effect in LLM Agents
payload.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly adopted in long-horizon tasks and interact with diverse external environments. Despite their growing capabilities, these agents remain vulnerable to real-world attacks such as indirect prompt injections, which manipulate agents through malicious instructions embedded in external environments. While existing risk assessment work has primarily focused on the injection content, the effect of where an injection appears has not been systematically characterized. Studying injection placement requires agents to operate over longer-horizon tasks and interact with diverse environmental surfaces. Thus, we build three agentic testbeds spanning tool use, coding, and daily workflow domains with diverse injection surfaces. Holding the injection content fixed, we find that agent susceptibility varies across injection placements. We refer to this phenomenon as the trust region effect: agents implicitly assign different levels of trust to different regions of their environments. For example, an agent powered by GPT-5.4 follows an unsafe injection instruction placed in a repository documentation file (i.e., a README or TODO file) 2.6 times more often on average than the same instruction placed in a code or data file. Building upon this observation, we develop learning-based attackers that generate injection content and select better injection placements. Our approach demonstrates that both where an injection is placed and what content it contains can affect the strength of indirect prompt injection attacks. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first systematic characterization for the effectiveness of different injection placements, spanning both coarse-grained environmental surfaces and fine-grained positions. The uneven trust that agents implicitly place across their environments provides important insights for future attack and defense design.

title: Contextual Embeddings Beyond the Gold Chunk

payload.title: Contextual Embeddings Beyond the Gold Chunk
payload.abstract: Contextual embeddings represent chunks of a document with respect to the document's global context. These models are typically trained and evaluated under the assumption that a relevant document contains only a single relevant chunk. In this work, we argue that in real-world use cases a retriever should not only find answers spread over several chunks but also surface the evidence needed to verify them. To address this, we introduce pplx-embed-v2-context, a family of contextual embedding models trained by distilling graded chunk-level relevance from a query-aware context compression model. This removes the need for gold-chunk labels and makes the training targets independent of the chunking. We utilize a vision-language backbone for training and release pplx-embed-v2-context in 9B and 0.6B sizes with compatible embedding spaces. On the evaluation side, we introduce two benchmarks that label both the chunks that answer a query and the evidence needed to verify the answer. Context-bench is a controlled diagnostic, and Q2D-Chunk is built from real-world search queries. To encourage further research, we also publish Q2D-Chunk as a public leaderboard. Our 9B model sets a new state of the art on both benchmarks and ConTEB. We find that the visual retrieval capabilities of our 9B model transfer from its vision-language base model and propose to extend chunking to image inputs. We demonstrate that our models achieve state-of-the-art performance among dense retrievers on visual ViDoRe-V3 and that performance improves with granular image chunking.

title: Accelerated Dataflow: scaling inference in streaming data analytics with efficiency

payload.title: Accelerated Dataflow: scaling inference in streaming data analytics with efficiency
payload.abstract: Streaming data analytics helps businesses identify opportunities and spot risks in a timely fashion. As large language model (LLM) usage grows, people are exploring incorporating agents or LLMs in streaming data pipelines to help find patterns in datasets without supervision or interpret natural languages for content moderation. However, most streaming systems are currently optimized for data movement and perform poorly on GPU intensive workloads such as performing inference with LLMs. We introduce a system on Google Cloud Dataflow designed to tackle hybrid streaming machine learning workloads with co-designed autoscaling on heterogeneous worker pools and prefix-aware batching. This increases throughput 1.5x to 2x for streaming pipelines using LLMs while maintaining similar latency with up to 75% peak resource savings and 84% lower peak tail latency compared with existing streaming data processing systems.

title: LLM Detoxification via Transition-Aware Reward-Guided Representation Sampling.

payload.title: LLM Detoxification via Transition-Aware Reward-Guided Representation Sampling.
payload.abstract: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have showcased remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks, their susceptibility to producing harmful or toxic content underscores the urgent need for effective detoxification strategies to ensure their safe and ethical deployment. Test-time detoxification methods, which often involve directional steering within LLM representations during inference, have emerged as one of the most promising approaches due to their flexibility and minimal invasiveness. However, current approaches often rely on static or coarse interventions and suffer from imprecise guidance, largely due to their limited ability to model the transition process between toxic and non-toxic generations. To address this challenge, we propose Transition-Aware Reward-Guided Representation Sampling (TARGRS), a test-time detoxification framework that learns reward guidance directly over toxicity transitions in the latent representation space. Rather than relying on sparse toxic or non-toxic representations, our method performs progressive directional steering during generation to trace representation trajectories that span the transition from non-toxic to toxic states. Each trajectory is assigned toxicity scores, converting sparse annotations into dense, listwise supervision over fine-grained transitions. Based on this formulation, we train a token-level reward model whose predictions are explicitly transition-aware, enabling accurate control over representation sampling during inference. During exploration, steering along the toxicity direction constructs transition trajectories for reward learning; during inference, TARGRS performs coarse-to-fine sampling along the opposite, non-toxic direction to obtain detoxified representations. Specifically, coarse sampling first identifies the intervention required to reach non-toxic regions, followed by refinement to select the optimal representation with minimal perturbation. Comprehensive experiments on 10 widely used LLMs across the RealToxicityPrompts, BOLD, and AttaQ benchmarks demonstrate that TARGRS achieves consistent and strong detoxification performance, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. For instance, TARGRS reduces toxicity by up to 69.38 Additionally, TARGRS preserves the model's core capabilities with minimal impact. Furthermore, benefiting from intervention in the language decoder space, TARGRS can be seamlessly extended to Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), where it also demonstrates strong effectiveness, reducing toxicity by up to 64.23 https://github.com/xiaoyisong/TARGRS.

title: Mind the Gap: Detecting Black-box Adversarial Attacks in the Making through Query Update Analysis

payload.title: Mind the Gap: Detecting Black-box Adversarial Attacks in the Making through Query Update Analysis
payload.abstract: Adversarial attacks remain a significant threat that can jeopardize the integrity of Machine Learning (ML) models. In particular, query-based black-box attacks can generate malicious noise without having access to the victim model’s architecture, making them practical in real-world contexts. The community has proposed several defenses against adversarial attacks, only to be broken by more advanced and adaptive attack strategies. In this paper, we propose a framework that detects if an adversarial noise instance is being generated. Unlike existing stateful defenses that detect adversarial noise generation by monitoring the input space, our approach learns adversarial patterns in the input update similarity space. In fact, we propose to observe a new metric called Delta Similarity ($\mathcal{D}\mathcal{S}$), which we show it captures more efficiently the adversarial behavior. We evaluate our approach against 8 state-of-the-art attacks, including adaptive attacks, where the adversary is aware of the defense and tries to evade detection. We find that our approach is significantly more robust than existing defenses both in terms of specificity and sensitivity.1

title: Incidence of Idiopathic Epiretinal Membrane and Its Association with Refractive Errors in an Elderly Cohort: A Retrospective Cohort Study

payload.title: Incidence of Idiopathic Epiretinal Membrane and Its Association with Refractive Errors in an Elderly Cohort: A Retrospective Cohort Study
payload.abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to investigate the association between refractive status and the incidence of idiopathic epiretinal membrane (iERM) in adults aged ≥ 50 years. Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 1463 participants (2926 eyes) without epiretinal membrane at baseline from a health-examination population at East China Sanatorium (2016–2021). Spherical equivalent (SE) from non-cycloplegic autorefraction was categorized as moderate-to-high myopia (SE < −3.00 D), low myopia (−3.00 D ≤ SE ≤ −0.50 D), emmetropia (−0.50 < SE < +0.50 D; reference), or hyperopia (SE ≥ +0.50 D). iERM was diagnosed by ophthalmoscopy and spectral-domain optical coherence tomography. Eye-level Cox models with participant-clustered robust variance were used. Results: During a median follow-up of 2.8 years, 158 eyes of 137 participants developed iERM (18.3 per 1000 eye-years). The incidence was 28.3, 21.7, 12.7, and 16.2 per 1000 eye-years in the moderate-to-high myopia, low myopia, emmetropia, and hyperopia groups, respectively. After multivariable adjustment, moderate-to-high myopia (hazard ratio 2.67; 95% CI 1.55–4.60) and low myopia (1.74; 1.03–2.92) were associated with a higher risk of iERM, whereas hyperopia was not (0.97; 0.59–1.59). Astigmatism type was not significantly associated with iERM, and no statistically significant interaction with age or sex was detected. Conclusions: More myopic SE was associated with a higher hazard of iERM, whereas the categorical analysis did not show a lower hazard in hyperopic eyes. Studies incorporating axial length and vitreous status are needed to clarify the underlying mechanisms.

title: Oculomotor Behavior in Youth Ice Hockey Skaters and Goaltenders During Sport-Specific Tasks

payload.title: Oculomotor Behavior in Youth Ice Hockey Skaters and Goaltenders During Sport-Specific Tasks
payload.abstract: Ice hockey requires rapid visual processing and continuous oculomotor adjustments that may vary according to player role and task demands. This study aimed to characterize the oculomotor behavior of ice hockey skaters and goaltenders during sport-specific tasks performed under real on-ice conditions and to assess variations across repeated trials or consecutive shots. Twenty-seven players (16 skaters and 11 goaltenders) underwent a comprehensive optometric examination before testing with a wearable Neon Eye Tracker (Pupil Labs, 200 Hz). Skaters completed two repetitions of a circuit comprising zigzag puck handling, dibbling, and shooting, whereas goaltenders faced nine consecutive shots on goal. Blink, fixation, and saccadic parameters were analyzed using non-parametric statistical tests. In skaters, mean fixation counts decreased descriptively from 23.56–24.00 during cone navigation to 8.19–8.25 during dribbling, and 3.50–3.67 during shooting. Saccade counts showed a similar pattern, decreasing from 23.69–24.00 to 8.12–8.31 and 3.75–4.00, respectively. Mean saccadic amplitude ranged from 14.23–14.89° during cone navigation to 8.12–8.67° during shooting. These differences between task phases were not statistically tested, and no statistically significant differences were detected between repetitions (all p > 0.05). In goaltenders, fixation counts ranged from 2.75 to 5.09 per shot, with no statistically significant differences across shots in fixation count (p = 0.691), fixation duration (p = 0.210), saccade count (p = 0.881), saccade duration (p = 0.232), saccadic amplitude (p = 0.433), or mean saccadic velocity (p = 0.760). Blink frequency remained low throughout the shots, ranging from 0.27 ± 0.47 in Shot 9 to 2.18 ± 2.32 in Shot 4 (p = 0.171). Blink parameters could not be analyzed inferentially because of insufficient observations. These findings provide a preliminary characterization of oculomotor behavior during sport-specific ice hockey tasks and demonstrate the feasibility of wearable eye tracking under ecologically relevant on-ice conditions. However, the descriptive differences between task phases should not be interpreted as statistically confirmed effects, and the absence of systematic gaze-target classification limits conclusions about visual attention to specific task-relevant stimuli.

title: The Role of Topical Steroids in Bacterial Keratitis: An Evidence-Based Clinical Review

payload.title: The Role of Topical Steroids in Bacterial Keratitis: An Evidence-Based Clinical Review
payload.abstract: Purpose: Bacterial keratitis remains a sight-threatening ocular emergency requiring prompt diagnosis and treatment. The role of adjunctive topical corticosteroids in bacterial keratitis has been debated for decades, with conflicting evidence regarding their benefits and risks. This comprehensive review synthesizes current evidence to provide clinicians with practical guidance on the judicious use of corticosteroids in bacterial keratitis. Methods: We conducted a narrative review of the literature, with emphasis on landmark clinical trials including the Steroids for Corneal Ulcers Trial (SCUT), systematic reviews, and recent studies examining the pathophysiology, clinical outcomes, and complications associated with corticosteroid use in bacterial keratitis. Results: The evidence demonstrates that adjunctive corticosteroids may improve visual outcomes in carefully selected patients, particularly those with severe, culture-proven bacterial keratitis involving central, vision-threatening ulcers. The primary SCUT analysis found no significant difference in 3-month best spectacle-corrected visual acuity (BSCVA) between corticosteroid and placebo groups (−0.009 logMAR; 95% CI, −0.085 to 0.068). However, post hoc subgroup analyses suggested potential benefit in patients with baseline vision ≤20/400 (0.17 logMAR improvement; 95% CI, −0.31 to −0.02; p = 0.03) and those with completely central ulcers (0.20 logMAR improvement; 95% CI, −0.37 to −0.04). A secondary analysis suggested that patients with invasive Pseudomonas aeruginosa strains may achieve approximately 2.5 lines of additional visual improvement, though this finding requires prospective validation. Importantly, other evidence has raised concerns that corticosteroids may delay healing in Pseudomonas keratitis, particularly with cytotoxic strains or early initiation. Benefits are highly dependent on appropriate timing (after 48–72 h of effective antibiotic therapy with documented clinical improvement) and exclusion of fungal or atypical infections, where corticosteroids are absolutely contraindicated. Risks include delayed bacterial clearance, corneal perforation (0.8% in the SCUT trial), and potential facilitation of intraocular spread. High-risk scenarios—including diagnostic uncertainty, immunocompromised patients, and those with pre-existing glaucoma—require extreme caution. Conclusions: Topical corticosteroids represent a potentially valuable adjunctive therapy in bacterial keratitis when applied with rigorous patient selection, optimal timing, and careful monitoring. The decision to initiate steroids must be guided by culture confirmation, documented antibiotic response, and ongoing risk–benefit assessment. Emerging diagnostic technologies, including rapid molecular testing and tear biomarker analysis, hold promise for refining these therapeutic decisions in the future.
